cohorts.summary: Early players debate the tense atmosphere against walking simulator pacing and confusing puzzles.

claims.claim: Reviewers mention that the game features a dark and tense atmosphere with well-designed environments and sound effects.

citations.review_text: Great story, quite surprising at times, atmosphere is dark and tense, nicely designed enviroment and sound efffects. For 2015 release this game has very low hardware requirements. Buy it for yourself or a friend as a gift, you won't regret it. I played it for many hours, not on record here. Well done game from this delevoper.

In my time with SOMA I felt conflicted... I liked the mysteries and atmosphere but I also felt like I was just kind of playing a walking sim. 

Additionally, I found the few enemies I encountered pretty boring. The red light robots in the ocean were pathetically easy to avoid and for some reason the first robot you encounter, the only kinda scary one, just kinda got stuck and let me move on. 

Another thing I find odd is some of the voice acting. Some of it's fine but then some deliveries are just totally off, like not the right amount of emotion is put into them. For example, two characters talk about someone dying and their tone just doesn't fit at all, plus they seem to move on almost instantly. 
I've played Amnesia TDD, Rebirth, and The Bunker and none of them had this issue with voice acting. It feels amateur at times, like the kind of voice acting I'd find in some much older game. 

TBH I'm probably just gonna watch a longplay on YouTube and refund this since I want to know some of the story stuff, I just don't think it's worth my money.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the enemy AI can feel easy to exploit or predictable, allowing players to run around monsters or easily avoid them.

citations.review_text: A pretty good horror game if you enjoy the "you can't defend yourself" type of gameplay. Enemy AI is fairly easy to exploit though and you can usually just run around them for the most part. Still, I would say it's worth a playthrough for the story.

Highly recommend, probably my favorite psychological horror game. The focus is on a lot of different questions about life, survival, and other immitations of life (such as robots and so on). Thankfully this game approaches this question completely in the opposite way to something like Detroit: Become Human, where the correct opinion is selected before you even play the game and you're emotionally railroaded to agree with it to get the best ending. 

This game asks you questions by giving you choices and then stands back for you to contemplate whether you did the correct thing. In the grand scheme of things the choices you make don't matter, because you are not the person affected by these choices. Only in the end do you realize how it really feels when the choice is made for you instead. Where you have no choice but to trust in fate or whatever high being you choose so that you get the best outcome. What an incredible story. 

Now a little nitpick here, most monsters are easy to deal with because the game tells you exactly how to deal with them. This isn't the case for all of the monsters, but it is for most of them. Takes the challenge out for no reason in my opinion.

Spoiler territory: [spoiler] Throughout the game you see robots revived using past memories of real people. Each and every one of them want to live and beg for their lives if you decide to shut them off. But the last and the only human that you meet wants you to end her life. Cinema. [/spoiler]

This game was made by the same developer that made Amnesia, which was revolutionary in it's own right. Compared to that, this game isn't as scary per se, but it is in fact a better game overall in every other aspect. This game relies much more on environmental thriller than anything else. Don't expect the usual jumpscare fest that other horror games heavily rely upon.

The gameplay consists of exploring levels and solving puzzles to progress while avoiding monsters. Very similar to Amnesia and Penumbra before it. But this time around, the visuals and storytelling have been massively improved. This game does NOT hold your hand, which can be frustrating for some people. No objective markers whatsoever, meaning you have to figure out everything for yourself. As mentioned earlier, you have to do this while avoiding the monsters, which I found quite easy to do by throwing something to distract them or simply stepping past them.

This game has a great sense of mood, atmosphere, and sound design. It's at it's scariest when you're simply walking around and experiencing the world. The real gem here is the story, which I won't spoil here but suffice to say it's extremely interesting in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up sort of way. Seriously, go experience this for yourself, it's damn good, and it'll leave you thinking about it long after you've beaten it.

As usual, this game is best experienced blind, alone, in the dark, and without distractions. Playing this with friends really hampers the experience, as it does most horror games. This was my favorite horror game I played last year, and still one of the best horror games I've ever played period. It's well worth the price point.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the stealth and monster encounter mechanics can feel frustrating, with enemies tracking player locations or repeating hide-and-seek sequences.

citations.review_text:
I have really mixed feelings about SOMA.

The story is genuinely incredible. The way it tackles consciousness and identity stuck with me way more than I expected and the ending has been living rent free in my head ever since. The atmosphere is amazing too. The lighting, sound design and environmental storytelling all come together to absolutely nail the existential horror vibe.

Then there's the gameplay.

I swear the monsters have my location open on Google Maps.

I'd spend ages sneaking around, hiding, breaking line of sight and trying to play smart only for the AI to somehow know exactly where I was anyway. After a while it stopped being scary and just became frustrating because it felt like the game had already decided how the encounter was going to play out. The scripted sequences didn't help either since I ended up worrying more about invisible triggers than the monsters themselves.

Even with all that I still think SOMA is absolutely worth playing. The story alone makes it an easy recommendation and it's one of those games that stays with you long after the credits. I just wish the enemy AI and scripted encounters rewarded stealth instead of making it feel pointless.

[b]Story:[/b] 10/10
[b]Atmosphere:[/b] 10/10
[b]Enemy AI:[/b] "I know where you live."
[b]Overall:[/b] 7/10. Great game frustrating stealth.

SOMA proves that great writing can only carry a video game so far. While Frictional Games crafts a deeply unsettling world with an incredible narrative, the actual experience of playing it quickly turns into a tedious chore.

[h3]The Good: Writing, Music, and Voice Acting[/h3]
The strengths here are undeniable. The writing is exceptional, delivering a thoughtful, existential sci-fi story that stays with you long after the credits roll. Every major beat is anchored by fantastic voice acting that brings real emotion and authenticity to the characters. Complementing the story is a standout music score and audio design that builds an oppressively atmospheric, isolated mood. The graphics are decent—nothing mind-blowing, but effective enough at rendering the dark, decaying halls of the PATHOS-II facility.

[h3]Why It Falls Apart: The Gameplay[/h3]
Despite the narrative strengths, the overall experience fails because the gameplay is painfully basic and boring. Rather than creating meaningful tension, the moment-to-moment mechanics boil down to linear fetch tasks and sluggish, repetitive hide-and-seek stealth with annoying monster encounters. Instead of complementing the story, the gameplay actively sabotages it, feeling like an artificial roadblock designed to pad out the runtime.

[h3]Verdict[/h3]
SOMA has the narrative backbone, voice talent, and audio design of a masterpiece, but a game still needs to be engaging to play. When the primary interactive elements feel like a sluggish drag, even the best writing can't save the experience from being a frustrating disappointment.

Rating: 2/5

After reading the reviews and being a long‑time fan of horror games, I figured SOMA would be right up my alley. I don’t mind slower, narrative‑focused games, but SOMA’s gameplay often worked against its own excellent story, making it harder for the narrative to land the way it should have.

Unfortunately, I walked away really disappointed. The story is fantastic — the only thing that kept me going after the first 15 minutes — but everything surrounding it fell flat for me.

The pacing is artificially slow in many aspects. Ladder climbing, underwater movement, door cycling, water‑draining sequences, carrying *an important late-game item*, even basic traversal all feel deliberately dragged out just to stretch a short narrative into a much longer runtime. On top of that, direction is often unclear, leading to running back and forth through the same rooms multiple times looking for tiny interactables. You can open nearly every drawer, locker, and cabinet in the game, but almost none of it serves any purpose. Yes, you can pick up almost everything — but you only ever use that ability twice.. The rest is just empty interactivity meant to look deep but adds nothing.

Gameplay is nearly nonexistent. The monsters don’t add tension; they add downtime. Most encounters boil down to crouching in a corner for several minutes waiting for a patrol to pass, or simply sprinting past them because they pose little real threat. It felt like they exist to slow you down, not to challenge you.

The puzzles are basic, usually amounting to “press buttons until the lights turn green.” They require little thought, 
 and feel more like speed bumps than actual problem‑solving.

Level design is repetitive, with the majority of the game taking place in same‑looking underwater environments. There’s very little visual or mechanical variety to keep you engaged.

Combine all of this with the fact that your choices have zero impact on the story, and the experience becomes pretty underwhelming. Calling …

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game offers a safety mode option at the start that makes monsters harmless.

citations.review_text: There is an option at the start of the game that selects if you want the monsters in the game to be able to harm you. You can thus select the setting that makes them harmless if you don't want to be bothered by the monsters, the option which I happily selected. Big thumbs up for the developer for introducing this option. I would not have liked the game as much as I did if this option was not available.

Cool narrative experience, the story of which explores topics of mortality, consciousness and the self in a very memorable way.

Gameplay wise it's mostly a walking simulator with light puzzle elements. There are some particularly obnoxious run-and-hide stealth sequences that don't add much other than generic "horror" aspects, and in hindsight I would really have preferred to play through the game with the safe mode enabled to skip through this.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the gameplay as minimal, functioning largely as a walking simulator focused on environmental exploration, reading lore, and solving straightforward puzzles.

citations.review_text: This game has one of the most devastating, beautiful, heartbreaking narratives, but most people will never open themselves up to it.  I got lucky and experienced this exactly the way it was intended, and it spoke to me.  This is a great story for the information age, I recommend it to anyone that loves reading Sci-fi horror as a genre.  It's a walking simulator at the end of the day, but a very good one, with surprisingly great graphics in 2026, the art, atmosphere and meticulously crafted audio soundscape carries it entirely.  It still holds up.  Full disclosure, if this one grabs you the way it grabbed me, you'll end it crying a little bit, and it will leave you feeling like a shell of your former self.  If you're not into that sort of thing, there are better ways to spend your time.  For me?  10/10, and indeed the only game I've ever felt the need to 100%.  Well, except for Dead Space, but that's another story entirely.

SOMA explores very interesting and existential ideas that progressively develop as the game advances, turning more compelling and disturbing, and reaching a high note at the end. The atmosphere throughout the game is claustrophobic and the deep sea setting is very well realized.

The gameplay, though, is a different story, and it's easily the least attractive part. It's a mix of walking simulator, puzzle solving, and parts where you have to dodge or run from enemies (there is zero combat), which can become tedious at times. On top of that, despite the narrative being quite interesting and rich, it is a bit over-explained sometimes. I feel that they could have left some things open to interpretation, a tad more open or at least not explained over and over.

Still, I find SOMA definitely worth it and would recommend it if you want a narrative, thoughtful game. One that will make for a nice conversation with friends.

It is a good game, however I don't really understand why it is so "life changing" for some folks. It is great to see the game that philosophizes on themes of conciousness and what does it mean to be a human, and I wish more games touched these topics, but at the same time, if you are into sci-fi, or just been thinking about conciousness from time to time, the main plot will be predictable. 

I think the side story and worldbuilding are more interesting in this game. Reading jouranls, listening for memories of people is truly interesting, it has been a while since I really wanted to read in the game, it doesn't feel like a filler, more like a separate plot inside the main plot.

The gameplay itself is alright, it is noting special: you walk, you talk, you read, you listen, solve puzzles -> then you run from monster -> you walk, you talk, you read, you listen, solve puzzles -> ... reapeat 10 times. The level design, atmosphere, is truly amazing, sounds are belivable, creepy, have true volume. 

I believe you should play this game, slowly, feel it, it is good ground to start thinking about what are you, what makes you you. 

Just don't make a cult around it.

claims.claim: Reviewers experience technical issues where high monitor refresh rates cause problems, requiring VSYNC to be turned on or refresh rates to be lowered to 60Hz.

citations.review_text: Bought SOMA ages ago and didn't play it because the performance was bad. The issue was simple, if your monitor is on anything higher than 60hz it hates it. But after finally getting passed that this is easily one of my favourite games and I won't stop thinking about it.

Absolutely beautiful game with an amazing story line that you piece together as you play the game. The emotions of characters are perfectly portrayed throughout the game. If I didn't know SOMA was made in 2015 I would have thought it was released in either 2025 or 2026. Environment is so beautiful and the dev team has perfectly portrayed the loneliness and isolation of the world where SOMA is set in. 

10/10 a must play, cus it was a journey much more than a game.


BTW if your game is lagging despite having a high end rig or can handle the game without an issue, here's the fix :

1. Turn on VSYNC
2. Make sure the game's refresh rate is lowered to 60 via in game settings

claims.claim: The game includes an option to toggle or disable the monsters during gameplay.

citations.review_text: I finished this game nine years ago and still think about it regularly. Play it for the story; Frictional was kind enough to have an option to toggle the monsters.

This is a story driven game with so-so mechanics. The artwork and levels are good. You have the option to play with danger or story focused. I'm glad I turned off the danger because I wouldn't have enjoyed it since all you could do is play stealth. 

There is a psychological/philosophical twist that some people may really enjoy so the game might be good for some people, but I was pretty bored by the end. I did like that most of the puzzles were fairly easy to solve so.
